options.A: The emission of electrons from the surface of a heated metal.
options.B: The emission of electrons when light falls on a metal.
options.C: The emission of light from a hot gas.
options.D: The emission of alpha particles from a nucleus.

questions.solution: Heating a metal gives some of its free electrons enough kinetic energy to escape from the surface. This is thermionic emission, used in electron guns. Emission caused by light is the photoelectric effect.

questions.q: An electron is accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 1000 V. What is its final speed? (\(e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{C}\), \(m_{e} = 9.11 \times 10^{-31}\ \text{kg}\))
questions.solution: The work done by the field becomes kinetic energy: \(\frac{1}{2}mv^{2} = eV\). So \(v = \sqrt{\frac{2eV}{m}} = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 1.60 \times 10^{-19} \times 1000}{9.11 \times 10^{-31}}} = 1.9 \times 10^{7}\ \text{m s}^{-1}\).

questions.q: Thomson found that the specific charge of cathode ray particles was about 1800 times that of the hydrogen ion. What was the significance of this?

options.A: It showed that cathode rays are a form of light.
options.B: It showed that cathode rays are particles much lighter than the lightest atom.
options.C: It showed that charge is quantised.
options.D: It showed that atoms have a nucleus.

questions.solution: A much larger charge-to-mass ratio than the hydrogen ion meant the particles had either a far larger charge or a far smaller mass. It was the first evidence of a particle smaller than an atom: the electron. Quantisation of charge came later, from Millikan.

questions.q: Electrons pass undeflected through an electric field of \(2.0 \times 10^{4}\ \text{V m}^{-1}\) crossed with a magnetic field of \(1.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{T}\). What is their speed?
questions.solution: Undeflected means the electric and magnetic forces balance: \(eE = Bev\). So \(v = \frac{E}{B} = \frac{2.0 \times 10^{4}}{1.0 \times 10^{-3}} = 2.0 \times 10^{7}\ \text{m s}^{-1}\).

questions.q: An oil droplet of mass \(9.8 \times 10^{-16}\ \text{kg}\) is held stationary between horizontal plates 5.0 mm apart with 300 V across them. What is the charge on the droplet? (\(g = 9.81\ \text{N kg}^{-1}\))
questions.solution: The electric force balances the weight: \(\frac{QV}{d} = mg\). So \(Q = \frac{mgd}{V} = \frac{9.8 \times 10^{-16} \times 9.81 \times 5.0 \times 10^{-3}}{300} = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{C}\), the charge of one electron.

questions.q: What did Millikan's oil drop experiment show?

options.B: The speed of light is the same for all observers.
options.D: Electric charge comes in whole-number multiples of a smallest amount.

questions.solution: The charge on every droplet was a whole-number multiple of \(1.6 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{C}\). So charge is quantised, and this smallest amount is the charge of the electron.

questions.q: What did Newton's corpuscular theory predict about the speed of light in glass compared with air?

options.C: Light travels at the same speed in both.

questions.solution: Newton explained refraction by saying that corpuscles are attracted towards the glass as they enter it, which would speed them up. Huygens' wave theory needed light to slow down in glass. Later measurements showed that light is slower in denser media, supporting the wave theory.

questions.q: Why was Young's double slits experiment important?

options.A: It measured the speed of light.
options.B: It showed that light is made of particles.
options.C: It showed light interfering, which supports a wave theory.
options.D: It showed that light can be polarised.

questions.solution: The pattern of many bright and dark fringes can only be explained by waves from the two slits reinforcing and cancelling. Particles would give just two bright bands. Even so, Newton's reputation delayed acceptance of the wave theory.

questions.q: Maxwell's formula gives the speed of electromagnetic waves in a vacuum in terms of two constants. Which are they?

options.A: The Planck constant and the charge of the electron.
options.B: The permeability of free space and the permittivity of free space.
options.C: The gravitational constant and the mass of the electron.
options.D: The Boltzmann constant and the Avogadro constant.

questions.solution: \(c = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_{0}\varepsilon_{0}}}\). The permeability of free space relates to magnetic fields around currents, and the permittivity of free space to electric fields around charges. The value matched the measured speed of light, showing that light is an electromagnetic wave.

questions.q: How did Hertz find the wavelength of the radio waves he produced?

options.A: By timing them over a known distance.
options.B: By passing them through a prism.
options.C: By setting up stationary waves with a reflector and measuring the distance between nodes.
options.D: By measuring the size of the spark gap.

questions.solution: Hertz reflected his radio waves from a metal sheet to form stationary waves. Adjacent nodes are half a wavelength apart, so their spacing gave the wavelength. With the frequency of his circuit, this gave a speed equal to that of light.

questions.q: The graph shows the measured radiation from a black body and the prediction of classical wave theory, which fails at short wavelengths (the ultraviolet catastrophe). How did Planck resolve this?

figure.alt: Intensity against wavelength. The measured curve rises to a peak and falls to zero at short wavelengths. The classical prediction, drawn dashed, agrees at long wavelengths but keeps rising steeply as the wavelength gets shorter.

options.A: By treating light as a stream of corpuscles attracted to matter.
options.B: By suggesting that hot bodies emit no ultraviolet radiation.
options.C: By treating radiation as a continuous wave.
options.D: By proposing that radiation is emitted in discrete quanta of energy proportional to frequency.

questions.solution: Classical theory predicted ever more radiation at shorter wavelengths, which does not happen. Planck proposed that energy is emitted only in packets of \(E = hf\). High-frequency quanta need a lot of energy, so few are emitted, and the curve falls at short wavelengths as observed.

questions.q: What is the de Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated from rest through 100 V? (\(h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s}\), \(e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{C}\), \(m_{e} = 9.11 \times 10^{-31}\ \text{kg}\))
questions.solution: \(\lambda = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2meV}}\). The momentum is \(\sqrt{2 \times 9.11 \times 10^{-31} \times 1.60 \times 10^{-19} \times 100} = 5.40 \times 10^{-24}\ \text{kg m s}^{-1}\). So \(\lambda = \frac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{5.40 \times 10^{-24}} = 1.2 \times 10^{-10}\ \text{m}\).

questions.q: What does a scanning tunnelling microscope rely on?

options.A: Electrons being focused by magnetic lenses after passing through a thin sample.
options.B: Electrons tunnelling across a tiny gap between a fine tip and a surface.
options.C: Light being reflected from the surface.
options.D: X-rays being diffracted by the surface.

questions.solution: Because electrons have a wave nature, they can tunnel across a gap of about a nanometre between a fine metal tip and a conducting surface. The tunnelling current is very sensitive to the width of the gap, so scanning the tip maps the surface atom by atom. Magnetic lenses belong to the transmission electron microscope.

questions.q: What was the result of the Michelson–Morley experiment, and what did it show?

options.A: The fringes shifted, showing that the Earth moves through the ether.
options.B: No fringes were seen, showing that light is not a wave.
options.C: The fringes shifted, showing that the speed of light depends on direction.
options.D: The fringes did not shift, showing that the speed of light does not depend on the motion of the observer.

questions.solution: If the Earth moved through an ether, rotating the interferometer should have shifted the fringes. No shift was found. So absolute motion cannot be detected, there is no ether, and the speed of light is invariant.

questions.q: A clock moves at \(0.60c\) relative to an observer. An interval of 8.0 s passes on the moving clock. How long is the interval according to the observer?
questions.solution: The 8.0 s is the proper time. \(t = \frac{t_{0}}{\sqrt{1 - \frac{v^{2}}{c^{2}}}}\), and \(\sqrt{1 - 0.60^{2}} = 0.80\). So t = 8.0 ÷ 0.80 = 10 s. Moving clocks run slow, so the observer always measures the longer time.

questions.q: A rod of proper length 50 m moves at \(0.80c\) along its length relative to an observer. What length does the observer measure?
questions.solution: \(l = l_{0}\sqrt{1 - \frac{v^{2}}{c^{2}}}\), and \(\sqrt{1 - 0.80^{2}} = 0.60\). So l = 50 × 0.60 = 30 m. A moving object is always measured as shorter along its direction of motion.
